Article Title: Quote of the day by Bill Gates: 'I believe that if you show people the problems and you show them the solutions, they will be moved to act'
Article Text:
“I believe that if you show people the problems and you show them the solutions, they will be moved to act.”

Quote of the day

“I believe that if you show people the problems and you show them the solutions, they will be moved to act.” Bill Gates

What the quote actually means

Who is the customer

What are their needs and priorities

What's happening in the market

What are competitors doing

What are our options for responding

How do we differentiate

How is technology changing and what possibilities does it offer customers

What are the business priorities

Why this mindset is more important than it seems

“Here is what is wrong,”

“Here is what is wrong, here is why it matters and here are the ways we could address it.”

We all come across problems that can feel too complicated, distant or difficult to solve. Whether it is a challenge at work, a business problem, or a larger issue affecting society, simply pointing out that something is wrong doesn't always lead to action. People are more likely to respond when they understand both the problem and what can be done about it.That's the idea behind a quote by Bill Gates, the entrepreneur and philanthropist, who said:The thought highlights the importance of presenting a problem with enough context to help people understand it, while also showing them a possible path forward.Gates' statement is closely connected to framing a problem. A problem can look very different depending on how it is presented, just like a picture can look different depending on how it is framed.Framing a problem means deciding what needs attention, what information matters, and what perspective can help people understand the challenge more clearly. It also puts boundaries around the problem, making it easier to examine rather than treating it as one large, undefined issue.But framing is not only about identifying what is wrong. It is also about putting the problem into context and showing people their options.For example, instead of simply saying a business is losing customers, a better approach is to look at who those customers are, what they need, what is changing in the market, and what competitors are doing differently.Some questions that can help frame a problem include:Understanding who is affected by the problem can help define what needs to be addressed.Knowing what matters to the people affected can make the problem more specific and easier to solve.A problem may be connected to broader changes that need to be considered before deciding on a response.Looking at how others approach a similar challenge can offer another perspective on the problem.Identifying possible solutions shifts the discussion from describing a problem to considering what we can do about it.Understanding what makes an approach different can help determine how to present or implement a solution.Technology can change both the nature of a problem and the solutions available to address it.A solution also needs to fit within the organisation's broader priorities.It is easy to tell people that something needs to change. It is much harder to get them to understand why it matters and what they can actually do about it.That is where framing becomes important. A problem presented without context can feel overwhelming or irrelevant. But when people can see the problem clearly and understand the possible solutions, they have a better basis for deciding how to respond.The same approach can apply to everyday challenges. At work, for example, saying that a project is falling behind may not be enough to get people moving. Explaining what is causing the delay, who is affected and what options are available gives the team a clearer picture of the situation.The idea also changes the way we communicate problems. Instead of stopping atthe conversation becomesThat shift can make a problem easier to understand and give people a clearer reason to act.
Article Summary: Bill Gates said: “I believe that if you show people the problems and you show them the solutions, they will be moved to act.” Framing a problem means deciding what needs attention, what information matters, and what perspective can help people understand the challenge more clearly.

Article Title: Inside Amazon India’s playbook for the Great Indian Festival 2026
Article Text:
Zeba Khan, Director of Consumer Electronics at Amazon India

In a conversation with The Times of India, Zeba Khan, Director of Consumer Electronics at

Amazon India

"To make our delivery experience more integrated and seamless, we have our Unified Delivery Service across over 300 cities, alongside, we have recently introduced Open Box Delivery on eligible high-value products will allow customers to verify the product at the time of delivery before accepting it. Together, these offerings bring greater choice, value, discovery and convenience to customers this festive season." Zeba Khan, Director of Consumer Electronics at Amazon India

‘Rising component costs has not dented premium ambitions’

‘AI popularity moves beyond smartphones’

Amazon Great India Festival dates

India’s consumer electronics landscape is seemingly seeing a decisive shift. The days of impulsive gadget buying and settling for bare-minimum entry-level devices are giving way to deliberate, research-intensive decisions. As households gear up for the festive season, shoppers are demanding premium hardware, tangible artificial intelligence capabilities, and transparent value., spoke about the emerging trends driving tech adoption across the country, drawing insights from the platform’s 'Best in Tech' Survey."As customers become more deliberate and research-led in their technology purchases, the Best in Tech Survey was conducted to understand the features, innovations and value propositions that matter most to them across categories," Khan explained. The survey, based on 40,000-plus responses across primary consumer electronics categories, revealed that consumer priorities have fractured into distinct, highly specialized buckets.In the smartphone arena, the baseline expectations, as per Amazon survey, remain rooted in speed and battery stamina, with raw performance leading the pack. Yet, emerging software capabilities are swiftly ascending the priority list.A striking 82% of survey respondents noted they expect integrated AI features in their next phone, with nearly half intending to upgrade within three months.A parallel evolution is taking place in personal computing. Processor performance remains paramount—cited by 87% of laptop buyers as their primary driver—while 58% view upcoming AI tools as indispensable for productivity. Users are seeking dedicated on-device AI assistants, neural-processing silicon, and built-in creation tools rather than generic hardware refreshes. Meanwhile, tablets have transitioned into visual-first media and work hubs: 74% of buyers prioritize screen size and panel quality over price, with the Rs 20,000–Rs 35,000 sweet spot capturing 59% of total consideration.The electronics industry has weathered consecutive waves of inflationary pressure driven by surging memory and chipset costs. Yet, rather than trading down to cheaper alternatives, Indian consumers are exercising patience. "There is no doubt that prices are rising and customers have seen several rounds of pricing increases due to higher chip and memory costs. At the same time, we are seeing a lot of pent-up demand, with customers holding on to their upgrades rather than compromising on what they want. Premiumisation is not going away," said Khan.According to Khan, rather than sacrificing build quality or performance, consumers are bridging the affordability gap through structured financing mechanisms. Exchange schemes, bank tie-ups, instant credit via Amazon Pay, and No-Cost EMI plans have evolved into essential purchasing levers. For large appliances, 47% of consumers identify No-Cost EMI as their single most critical pricing enabler."Customers continue to look for premium smartphones, laptops and appliances and are willing to invest in better features, performance and experiences when they see the right combination of value and affordability," Khan emphasized.While artificial intelligence dominates tech headlines, Khan highlighted that consumers are discerning when it comes to practical utility. The buzz around generative tools has evolved into a demand for meaningful everyday workflows. "We are seeing growing interest in AI across categories. Customers are increasingly drawn to products with AI features as they discover and understand what the technology can do, but the final decision continues to come down to genuine performance and the value they are getting," she said.Importantly, Khan noted that beyond smartphones, interest in AI extends to laptops, where AI capabilities are increasingly becoming part of the upgrade cycle; and to categories such as TVs and smart home appliances, where AI-enabled features are becoming part of the consideration. The broader trend is towards customers looking for technology that is relevant to their specific use cases, whether that is gaming, creation, work or everyday use. She said, "It definitely extends beyond smartphones. On smartphones, AI features are becoming increasingly important as customers discover and understand what the technology can do, but they continue to evaluate the device on fundamentals such as camera, processing speed and everyday performance. Beyond smartphones, we are seeing this interest extend to laptops... and to categories such as TVs and smart home appliances."Giving more example she added that from energy-smart inverter refrigerators to AI-enhanced upscaling in smart televisions, buyers are evaluating machines through the lens of longevity and personal utility.To meet increase in demand as it heads into the Amazon Great Indian Festival 2026, the e-commerce giant is overhauling both discovery and post-purchase fulfillment. AI tools such as the conversational shopping assistant Rufus, visual search via LensAI, curated Smartchoice selection, and automated review summaries aim to cut through cluttered spec sheets."This festive season, we are focused on making product discovery easier and helping customers make more confident decisions," Khan noted, pointing out that peace of mind extends all the way to the doorstep. "Customers can benefit from open-box delivery on eligible products, giving them the opportunity to verify the product at the time of delivery. Our installation services are available across over 300 cities, helping customers get their appliances set up conveniently after purchase. "Amazon Great Indian Festival starts on October 8, 2026. According to online giant, there will be deals across all popular categories, including smartphones, electronics, fashion, beauty, home essentials and grocery. Customers also get a 10% instant discount on SBI Credit and Debit Cards and EMI transactions, and up to 10% extra only for Prime members.
Article Summary: Zeba Khan, Director of Consumer Electronics at Amazon India, spoke about the emerging trends driving tech adoption across the country. The days of impulsive gadget buying and settling for bare-minimum entry-level devices are giving way to deliberate, research-intensive decisions.

Article Title: Nike cofounder Phil Knight makes largest known donation to public flagship university, made over an unscheduled call, University president calls the 'extraordinary gift an endorsement of ...'
Article Text:
Nike co-founder Phil Knight

Nike co-founder has given billions to Oregon causes

Phil Knight’s donation comes as US university funding faces uncertainty

Nike cofounder Phil Knight just made the largest known donation to a public flagship university in the US. According to a New York Times report, Phil Knight and his wife Penny have donated a whopping $1 billion to the University of Oregon. The donation, surfaced from an unscheduled call, will go toward establishing an engineering college in the University. The latest pledge adds to previous donations by the Knights. Last week, they committed $1.1 billion to Providence St. Vincent Medical Center and Providence Heart Institute in Portland. In 2025, they gave $2 billion to OHSU’s Knight Cancer Institute. Knight, 88, has a net worth of nearly $23 billion, according to Bloomberg.Responding to the donation, Karl Scholz, president of the University of Oregon, told Fortune: “This extraordinary gift is an endorsement of what higher education delivers. It gives us the ability to scale innovation, accelerate impact, and meet the demand for skilled engineering required by the industries of tomorrow, all without placing that financial burden on state taxpayers.”The couple has also made major donations linked to University of Oregon athletics.They have previously given $100 million to build the university’s basketball arena, named in honour of their late son, Matthew Knight.Phil Knight’s support has also helped create strong ties between the university and Nike. Oregon athletes have access to new and exclusive Nike gear, along with support related to name, image and likeness (NIL) deals. Because of the close relationship, some people call Oregon the “University of Nike.”Phil Knights’ donation comes as federal support for universities faces uncertainty. In early 2025, the Trump administration laid off thousands of workers at federal science agencies, delayed some grant payments to universities and sought cuts to funding for research overheads. The administration also withdrew some DEI grants.Additionally, the White House’s fiscal 2026 budget proposal called for a nearly 36% cut in non-defense science research and development funding. It also proposed cuts of nearly 57% at the National Science Foundation (NSF) and more than 40% at the National Institutes of Health (NIH). However, Congress largely rejected those proposed cuts and kept science funding mostly unchanged.
Article Summary: Phil Knight and his wife Penny have donated a whopping $1 billion to the University of Oregon. The donation, surfaced from an unscheduled call, will go toward establishing an engineering college in the University. Knight, 88, has a net worth of nearly $23 billion, according to Bloomberg.

Article Title: As Nokia is closing its research hub in China; it is back to the time when Nokia CEO asked Europe: Why you use Huawei, while China has thrown us out
Article Text:
Nokia new logo

Nokia's China revenue has more than halved since 2018

Huawei still runs around 60% of Germany's 5G sites

Nokia's AI and cloud orders are booming as its RAN business shrinks

Nokia has confirmed it is winding down its radio technology research and development centre in Hangzhou by the end of 2026, cutting roughly 1,600 jobs and quietly closing the book on a China strategy that has been unravelling for the better part of a decade. Staff were told on Thursday, August 13. The company's explanation was clinical—it is aligning its China operations with how Nokia works globally, and its business there has been shrinking for years. Light Reading reports that Nokia sites in Beijing, Chengdu, Qingdao and Shanghai could follow, though the company hasn't confirmed that.What makes the timing interesting is the argument it revives. In September 2025, at a press conference in Oulu, Finland, Nokia CEO Justin Hotard asked Europe a question it still hasn't properly answered: "Why do we allow high-risk vendors in Europe in our networks," he said, when Nokia holds under 3% share in China? Nokia executives said at the time they had been told European vendors were to be pushed out of China on national security grounds. The Hangzhou shutdown is what that warning looks like on the ground.The numbers explain the exit better than any statement does. Nokia's Greater China sales fell from nearly €2.2 billion in 2018 to €913 million in 2025—a drop of more than 58%. The turn came in 2020, when Nokia lost out on key radio access network contracts with China Mobile, China Telecom and China Unicom. What looked like a product problem then looks structural now.Danish analyst John Strand put it flatly in January: "China is lost land for vendors like Ericsson and Nokia. "Hotard's complaint about asymmetry hasn't aged. Huawei accounts for roughly 59% of Germany's 5G radio sites, according to Strand Consult data cited by the country's interior ministry. Only 13 of the EU's 27 member states had fully or partly adopted the bloc's 5G security toolbox as of 2025. Brussels is now moving to make it mandatory—a shift Hotard called "a very good and important step" in January. Germany wants Chinese components in RAN networks down to 25% by October 1, 2026.The retreat isn't cheap. Nokia raised its 2026 restructuring charge from €250 million to €800 million, with about €350 million tied to China and the integration of Nokia Shanghai Bell, which it bought out fully in December 2025. Headcount, around 103,000 in 2018, should end this year near 70,000.The other half of the story is happier. Second-quarter AI and cloud order intake hit €2.8 billion, up 105% year-on-year, and the stock is up 67% this year. Nokia is betting AI-RAN carries it into 6G. The catch: China is running 5G-Advanced across 330 cities, 12 to 18 months ahead of Western carriers, and Nokia will now build without that data.
Article Summary: Nokia has confirmed it is winding down its radio technology research and development centre in Hangzhou by the end of 2026. Nokia's Greater China sales fell from nearly €2.2 billion in 2018 to €913 million in 2025. Nokia raised its 2026 restructuring charge from €250 million to €800 million, with about €350 million tied to China.

Article Title: Sam Altman-backed Praxis plans $1 billion AI-powered town in Uruguay; first residents expected in mid-2027 with homes, resorts and cultural spaces for the AI era
Article Text:
An aerial concept rendering of Praxis’s proposed waterfront resort in Uruguay, featuring minimalist architecture, a swimming pool and landscaped surroundings. (Image: Praxis)

Sam Altman-backed Praxis selects Uruguay for its $1 billion AI-powered town

$1 billion investment planned over several years

First residents expected in mid-2027

Homes, resorts and cultural spaces planned

A community designed around the AI era

Sam Altman's connection to Praxis

+Colonia provides the physical foundation

Who is expected to live there?

The project remains in its early stages

Praxis, a technology-focused community backed by Apollo Projects, a fund associated with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, has selected Uruguay for its first physical development. The project involves a projected investment of about $1 billion in the +Colonia development near Colonia del Sacramento. The first Praxis residents are expected to arrive around mid-2027, while construction of the larger community continues over the following years. Plans include private residences, a resort and spaces for art, music and other cultural activities. Praxis presents the project as an experiment in how communities could live and organise in a future shaped by artificial intelligence.After searching for a location for about two years, Praxis chose +Colonia, a waterfront urban development near Colonia del Sacramento, as the home of its first physical community. The location offers access to the Río de la Plata and is close to both Montevideo and Buenos Aires. Eduardo Bastitta, founder of +Colonia, has described the partnership as an opportunity to bring together technology, entrepreneurship and new forms of community living.Praxis says its wider online community has more than 150,000 members, including entrepreneurs, investors and people working in technology and artificial intelligence.About 2,700 members have expressed interest in moving to or investing in the Uruguay project. Rather than creating a completely new city on undeveloped land, Praxis is establishing its community within the existing +Colonia development, where construction is already underway.The $1 billion figure attached to the project represents projected investment, rather than money already spent on construction. According to El País and El Observador, the initial Praxis area is expected to cover approximately 350,000 square metres, or roughly 20% of the planned +Colonia urbanisation.Much of the projected spending is expected to be connected to residences and other facilities that Praxis members will purchase or develop. The land transaction is also expected to progress in stages. El País reported that the land sale had not been completed when Praxis announced the project, meaning the full development remains dependent on subsequent agreements, purchases and construction.The first members of the Praxis community are expected to arrive at +Colonia around mid-2027, but that date does not represent the completion of the wider project.Instead, early residents are expected to move into buildings already being developed at +Colonia while the dedicated Praxis neighbourhood takes shape. This allows the community to establish a physical presence before the full range of planned facilities is completed.Dryden Brown, Praxis's co-founder and CEO, is also expected to relocate to Uruguay as the project gets underway.The proposed community is designed to combine residential life with hospitality and cultural activities. Praxis plans private residences, a resort and spaces for art and music, alongside studios, galleries and workshops.The company's vision also includes restaurants, nightlife venues, gardens, public squares, a waterfront promenade and a beach club. Photography, film and music production spaces are also planned, while fellowship programmes could bring artists, musicians, designers, writers and founders to the community.Concept images released by Praxis show minimalist buildings with large glass openings, landscaped areas and pools overlooking the waterfront. These remain proposed designs and do not guarantee that every structure shown will ultimately be built in the same form.The physical development is closely tied to Praxis's broader philosophy about the impact of artificial intelligence. The organisation says it wants to develop new cultural, economic and governance systems for what it describes as a post-AGI world.Its vision is centred on bringing together people involved in technology, entrepreneurship and creative fields and giving them a physical environment in which to live and collaborate as AI changes work and economic activity.However, the currently announced plans do not establish that the town will have AI-controlled utilities, autonomous transport or an AI-run government. The confirmed physical plans focus on housing, hospitality, cultural facilities and community spaces. In this context, the description of the project as “AI-powered” primarily reflects Praxis's technology-driven vision rather than a confirmed specification for all of its infrastructure.Altman's connection to the project comes through Apollo Projects, which Uruguayan media identify as a fund associated with the OpenAI CEO and one of Praxis's backers.That connection does not mean Altman personally owns or is directly developing the Uruguay project, nor does it mean OpenAI is building the community. Praxis is led by Brown, who has described the development as a way to explore how people might live, work and find purpose as artificial intelligence becomes increasingly influential.The involvement of an Altman-associated fund nevertheless places the project within the wider network of technology and AI investment that has emerged around the development of new communities and infrastructure.Praxis is entering a development that already exists rather than starting with an empty site. +Colonia is being built as a large waterfront community near Colonia del Sacramento, with construction already underway.The existing buildings provide a starting point for Praxis's first residents, while the dedicated neighbourhood can be developed progressively. According to El Observador, the initial Praxis area would account for roughly one-fifth of the broader +Colonia urbanisation.This arrangement also explains why the first residents can arrive in 2027 even though the larger project is expected to take considerably longer to develop.Praxis's wider community includes more than 150,000 people, but only a small portion are currently expected to relocate to Uruguay. Around 2,700 members have indicated interest in moving to or investing in the project.The proposed community is aimed at a mix of entrepreneurs, investors, technology professionals and creative workers. Alongside residential facilities, the planned studios, galleries, restaurants and cultural spaces are intended to encourage interaction between those groups.The result is intended to be less a conventional residential development and more a concentrated community built around technology, business and creative activity.Despite its ambitious scale and futuristic designs, the Praxis development remains an evolving project. The $1 billion figure is a projection for future investment, while land acquisition and construction are expected to proceed in stages.For now, the most immediate milestone is the planned arrival of the first Praxis residents around mid-2027. The larger neighbourhood, including its homes, resort and cultural facilities, is expected to take shape over the years that follow.If the plans proceed as announced, the Uruguay project will give Praxis its first permanent physical base and turn its vision of an AI-era community from an online experiment into a real-world development.
Article Summary: Praxis, a technology-focused community, has selected Uruguay for its first physical development. The project involves a projected investment of about $1 billion in the +Colonia development near Colonia del Sacramento. The first Praxis residents are expected to arrive around mid-2027. Plans include private residences, a resort and spaces for art, music and other cultural activities.

Article Title: McDonald's says its AI-enabled drive-thru system can now take orders in English and Spanish with 90% accuracy; it could save at least 50 labour hours a week; CFO Ian Borden notes that company has no i
Article Text:
$8.5 billion global modernization plan of McDonald’s

Archy and ArchIQ: AI at the center of the plan

Beyond AI: physical store upgrades

Menu changes driven by protein demand

Staying focused on value amid cost-of-living pressure

Employee training and customer value

McDonald’s announced that its AI-enabled drive-thru system called Archy can now take orders in both English and Spanish with 90% accuracy. According to a report by CBS, the company said that the system could save at least 50 labour hours per week at a typical restaurant by streamlining order-taking. CFO Ian Borden also stressed that the intention is not to reduce staff but to free employees to focus on hospitality and food preparation tasks, such as hand-breading chicken.The announcement came as McDonald’s unveiled a $8.5 billion investment plan over the next decade to modernize its 46,000 restaurants worldwide. CEO Chris Kempczinski said the company must improve productivity and capture market share in a flat fast-food traffic environment. Planned upgrades include lockers for delivery orders, redesigned kitchen layouts, bigger play areas, and more visible coffee preparation stations to enhance quality perceptions.A key piece of the modernization push is McDonald's AI-enabled drive-thru ordering system, Archy, which the company says can now take orders in both English and Spanish with 90% accuracy. According to CFO Ian Borden, the system could eventually save at least 50 labor hours per week at a typical restaurant.Importantly, Borden was clear that the goal isn't to cut staffing — instead, employees freed up from order-taking would be redirected toward hospitality-focused tasks or hands-on food preparation work, like hand-breading chicken.Archy operates alongside ArchIQ, a broader AI system McDonald's developed in partnership with Google that's designed to improve order accuracy while automating backend tasks like inventory management and staff scheduling. Kempczinski said early testing shows customers have responded well to Archy specifically because it makes their orders more accurate, adding that the company's approach to AI isn't rooted in treating the technology as inherently good or bad, but in being deliberate about how it's actually deployed.The modernization plan extends well past software. McDonald's said upcoming restaurant redesigns will include lockers for handling delivery orders, more visible coffee preparation areas meant to improve customers' perception of quality, larger play areas, and reworked kitchen layouts. Order-accuracy scales, already active in 10,000 restaurants globally, are set to expand to 20,000 locations by 2028.On the food side, McDonald's highlighted strong results from its hand-breaded chicken, currently rolled out across 10,000 restaurants in Asia and a small number of locations near Chicago, with plans to expand testing into additional US markets and Ireland next year — a category where rivals like Chick-fil-A and KFC have long had an edge. The company also plans to introduce grilled chicken sandwiches and wraps, along with experimenting with items like egg bites and bowls.Skye Anderson, president of McDonald's USA, tied this shift directly to changing consumer habits, noting that roughly 30 million Americans currently use GLP-1 weight loss drugs and are increasingly seeking smaller, protein-dense meals as a result. She pointed to internal research suggesting a much larger opportunity, though, with roughly 60 million Americans actively looking to add more protein to their diets overall — a gap she framed as a chance for McDonald's to give customers more reasons to choose the brand first.Despite the modernization push, Kempczinski emphasized that value remains central to McDonald's strategy, particularly for lower-income consumers. He defined low-income US households as those earning $45,000 or less annually, noting that while this group still eats fast food, they're doing so less frequently than before. He credited meal bundles like the $5 meal deal with helping address that pressure, and said McDonald's is exploring introducing entry-level pricing on a basic menu of items in the US, mirroring an approach it already uses in Europe and other markets. He described the current economic backdrop as one demanding constant attention to value, noting that cost-of-living pressure on consumers isn't going away anytime soon.McDonald’s is also rolling out new hospitality-focused training, showing employees what a perfectly cooked Big Mac tastes like and encouraging more pleasant customer interactions. At the same time, the company remains focused on value, exploring entry-level pricing for basic menu items in the U.S. to counter cost-of-living pressures.
Article Summary: McDonald’s announced that its AI-enabled drive-thru system called Archy can now take orders in both English and Spanish with 90% accuracy. The company said that the system could save at least 50 labour hours per week at a typical restaurant by streamlining order-taking. CFO Ian Borden stressed that the intention is not to reduce staff but to free employees to focus on hospitality and food preparation tasks, such as hand-breading chicken.

Article Title: In 2023, Jeff Bezos’ Earth Fund pledged $100 million for Pacific conservation; three years later, a new $25 million round is backing five nations to protect and manage 625,000 square miles of ocean
Article Text:
The Bezos Earth Fund began in 2020 and is guided by Jeff Bezos and Lauren Sánchez Bezos

Bezos Earth Fund backs five Pacific nations

In the Cook Islands, funding will help advance the country's Marae Moana ocean management plan, including expanding protections, improving monitoring and supporting local leadership.

In Kiribati, the funding will support marine spatial planning, identifying important ocean habitats, strengthening existing protected areas and improving monitoring and enforcement.

Papua New Guinea will use the support to work towards its first large offshore marine protected area and strengthen community stewardship of coastal waters.

In Tonga, the funding will help establish new protected areas and improve monitoring and enforcement. Tonga has set a goal of protecting 30% of its ocean.

In Vanuatu, the funding will support the implementation of its national marine spatial plan, including offshore conservation areas and community-led marine management.

Bezos Earth Fund also aims to support international waters

How the new $25 million links to Bezos' 2023 pledge

More Pacific countries are now involved

The Bezos Earth Fund is committing more than $25 million to ocean conservation projects across five Pacific nations. As stated in the official announcement, the latest funding will support conservation efforts in the Cook Islands, Kiribati, Papua New Guinea, Tonga and Vanuatu, as well as plans for marine protected areas in international waters. This covers more than 625,000 square miles of ocean, an area larger than Alaska. Noatbly, the funding is part of a larger $100 million commitment announced by the Bezos Earth Fund in 2023 to support the Pacific-led Unlocking Blue Pacific Prosperity initiative. With the latest grants, the fund, founded by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos , says it has now committed $63.3 million towards that pledge.The new grants will support different ocean conservation projects in five countries mentioned above.Notably, the latest donation by Jeff Bezos owned organization is not limited to waters controlled by individual countries. A separate grant to Rare will support Pacific governments in developing some of the world's first proposals for marine protected areas on the high seas.The UN High Seas Treaty entered into force in January 2026, creating a legal pathway for countries to establish marine protected areas in international waters.The Bezos Earth Fund said Pacific governments will work with regional experts to identify important high-seas areas and develop proposals for their protection.“Every kid falls in love with the ocean before anyone tells them it’s in trouble. I was that kid. I still am. This summer I spent time in the Pacific, and the water was everything you’d imagine. But what I keep coming back to is the people. Out there, the ocean isn’t just a beautiful view. It’s the road, the pantry, the backyard. They’ve been protecting it for generations because their lives depend on it. Nobody had to explain the stakes to them. So, this is us backing what they’ve already been doing. Five nations. Protection that lasts for generations to come,” said Lauren Sánchez Bezos, Vice Chair of the Bezos Earth Fund.The latest funding goes back to a commitment made by the Bezos Earth Fund at COP28 in 2023. At the time, the fund announced plans to provide up to $100 million to help Pacific Island leaders design and implement their Unlocking Blue Pacific Prosperity conservation plan.The initiative aims to sustainably manage 100% of the Blue Pacific Continent and protect at least 30% of the region by 2030. The 2023 announcement said the plan would protect more than 1 billion hectares of ocean and support the restoration of coral reefs, mangroves and other coastal ecosystems.The latest announcement marks the second round of funding under that $100 million commitment. The Earth Fund announced seven grants worth $37.5 million in 2025. With the new grants, its total funding under the Pacific commitment has reached $63.3 million.The Bezos Earth Fund said work from its earlier grants is already underway. Earlier this year, French Polynesia created a network of fully protected marine areas covering nearly 625,000 square miles of ocean.In Niue, where 40% of national waters are already protected, Earth Fund funding is supporting monitoring, enforcement and long-term financing.With the latest round, 17 of the Pacific's 22 countries and territories are now working on efforts to protect or sustainably manage their waters, according to the Bezos Earth Fund.
Article Summary: The Bezos Earth Fund is committing more than $25 million to ocean conservation projects across five Pacific nations. The latest funding will support conservation efforts in the Cook Islands, Kiribati, Papua New Guinea, Tonga and Vanuatu. This covers more than 625,000 square miles of ocean, an area larger than Alaska. With the latest grants, the fund has now committed $63.3 million towards that pledge.
